solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Address according to zip code?

blocks.note: surface reading: writing an address with the right postal code, the American zip code
setter's reading: a speech delivered in the language of zip, meaning energy and vigour, to rouse a team

explanation.surface: Someone checks they have written an envelope's address with the correct American postal code.
explanation.walkthrough: Zip here is liveliness, not a postcode, and the address is a speech rather than a place on an envelope.
explanation.definitionFit: A short rousing speech given to motivate players or staff before an effort is an address made to them.

clue.text: Ancient coach very bad, you might say

indicators.note: you might say signals the wordplay is spoken, so what counts is how it is pronounced

blocks.note: to prime is to coach or prepare someone, and evil is very bad

explanation.surface: Someone complains that an old coach, a bus perhaps, is in terrible shape.
explanation.walkthrough: Coach is the verb to train, not a vehicle or a sports trainer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes the earliest ages of the world, so it means belonging to remote antiquity, very old.

clue.text: The work of a features editor?

definitions.text: The work of a features editor?

blocks.clueFragment: The work of a features editor?
blocks.note: surface reading: the job of a newspaper journalist in charge of feature articles
setter's reading: someone who edits facial features, reshaping noses and chins in the operating theatre

explanation.surface: A description of what a newspaper's features editor does all day.
explanation.walkthrough: Features are parts of the face, and the editor is a surgeon who alters them.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic operations reshape the face and body, so the surgeon literally revises a patient's nose, lips or jaw.

clue.text: One winged beast stopped half-way

indicators.note: stopping half-way means only the first half is reached, so the second half is lost

blocks.note: a beast is an animal

explanation.surface: A flying monster halted in mid-journey.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'One winged', a thing with wings; winged beast is a false pairing.
explanation.definitionFit: The ani is a black tropical American bird of the cuckoo family, so it is one creature with wings.

clue.text: Some Africans know stories but run away

indicators.note: sent away means removed, so that letter goes

blocks.note: ken is Scots for know
yarns are tall stories
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Some Africans know tales but flee.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken is a Scots and northern dialect verb meaning to know; away tells you the run is removed from the stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Citizens of the East African republic whose capital is Nairobi are a particular group of people from the continent.

clue.text: Food scarce at safe houses

indicators.note: a phrase that houses something holds it inside, so the letters sit within the neighbouring words

blocks.note: running across the end of scarce, all of at and the start of safe

explanation.surface: Supplies are short in the safe houses where people are hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: Eats is informal slang for food, a meal or snacks, used as a plural noun.

clue.text: I bore myself over old lecturers

indicators.note: in a down clue over means turned upside down, so the letters go from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: taken as written
to bore someone is to tire them
me refers to myself

explanation.surface: A speaker admits they bore themselves when talking about retired academics.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string I TIRE ME is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired professors who keep their title honorarily are emeriti, the Latin plural of emeritus, so they are former teachers.

clue.text: People like Delilah supply hair?

blocks.note: a supply teacher is a temporary one, a temp
tresses are long locks of hair

explanation.surface: Women like Delilah, who cut Samson's locks, provide hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Supply is the noun from British supply teacher, a stand-in, not the verb to provide.
explanation.definitionFit: Delilah seduced Samson in the Bible to learn his secret, so she is the archetype of a seductive woman.

clue.text: Keen on traps being economical

blocks.note: a keen wind is a cutting one, sharp
to corner someone is to trap them

explanation.surface: Someone eager about traps that save money.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means doing something cheaply or skimping on quality to save money or effort.

clue.text: Turn left? No, this is fun

indicators.note: no means without, so the letter it qualifies is taken out

blocks.note: to wheel is to turn
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A driver asks about turning left and is told the ride is fun.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn left? looks like a driving question, but No strips the L from WHEEL.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is what people cry on a thrilling ride, expressing delight and excitement.

clue.text: It replaced aerial in TV, say

indicators.note: things replaced are put back in different places, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange
to mouth words is to say them

explanation.surface: Someone recalls the day a television's aerial was swapped for something else.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like a pronoun but is the definition: in a gin and it, the it is short for Italian vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: In bar slang the drink gin and it uses it as the standard abbreviation for the sweet Italian-made fortified wine.

clue.text: America’s past as a Time feature

definitions.text: America’s past as a Time feature

blocks.clueFragment: America’s past as a Time feature
blocks.note: surface reading: United States history written up as a story in Time magazine
setter's reading: the word Americans use in place of past when telling the clock, as in ten minutes this side of the hour

explanation.surface: A news magazine runs a feature on the history of the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: Time is not the magazine but clock time: where a Briton says ten past six, an American often says ten after six.
explanation.definitionFit: In American speech this preposition replaces past when stating minutes beyond the hour, so it is the US version.

clue.text: Forgiveness for what a monarch says?

blocks.note: first meaning: an official sovereign pardon cancelling a punishment
second meaning: a king or queen asking someone to repeat themselves

explanation.walkthrough: Pardon? is a polite request to repeat, so a king's version would be a regal one.
explanation.definitionFit: The sovereign's prerogative of mercy lets the Crown excuse a convicted person from a penalty.

clue.text: Noble title—it’s unwanted, he thought

indicators.note: what is unwanted is thrown out, so the word it is removed from the word beside it

blocks.note: short for aristocrat, a noble
taken as written
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A thinker reflects that an aristocrat's title is not wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noble title' reads as one phrase, a peerage, but noble is a separate piece; the definition is the closing 'he thought', meaning a thinker.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek philosopher is a famous thinker, so he is the man who thought; the clue's 'he thought' points to him.

clue.text: Failing to include endless herb is good for soup

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is dropped from the herb's name
including something means holding it inside, so one word wraps around the others

blocks.note: a vice is a moral failing
hyssop is an aromatic herb
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardening tip says that a bad herb crop can still flavour soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good for' is a link meaning the wordplay suits the definition; the herb loses its last letter before being placed inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Vichyssoise is a thick creamy leek and potato soup, usually served chilled, so it is an example of soup.

clue.text: Almost pull over? Indeed

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
turned over, the letters are read from the other end

blocks.note: to yank is to pull sharply

explanation.surface: A driver nearly pulls over to the roadside, and someone agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: Nay is the old intensifier meaning not only that but more, as in 'it was difficult, nay impossible'.
explanation.definitionFit: Used to strengthen a statement, the archaic word works like 'and more than that', which matches the emphatic sense of indeed.

clue.text: Old song that makes me happy about windy desert

indicators.note: windy suggests being blown about, so these letters are scattered
about means around, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: yay is a cry of happiness
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone names an old tune that cheers them up, about a windswept desert.
explanation.walkthrough: The Beatles' song of 1965 is the old song in question.
explanation.definitionFit: Yesterday is a much-covered Paul McCartney ballad from the 1960s, so it is a classic tune.

clue.text: Currency of central Europe

indicators.note: of marks letters that are taken out of the following words rather than standing for a meaning

blocks.note: spanning the end of central and the start of Europe

explanation.surface: A question about which money is used in the middle of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer really is a European currency, so the surface is also true.
explanation.definitionFit: The leu is the monetary unit of Romania and of Moldova, so it is a national currency.

clue.text: Wild cats, felines, camouflaged creatures

indicators.note: wild suggests running out of control, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A list of animals: big cats and other felines, hidden by their markings.
explanation.definitionFit: These tropical bugs have flattened green bodies that mimic foliage, so they are hidden by disguise from predators.

clue.text: Funny old lady back on drugs?

indicators.note: going back means the letters run in the opposite direction

blocks.note: old lady is slang for mother, ma
using is slang for taking drugs

explanation.surface: Is it funny that an old woman is back on narcotics?
explanation.definitionFit: Something that causes laughter or entertains is comical, the adjective sense of the word.

clue.text: Skating event is entertaining church, and how!

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them in, so one word takes the other inside

blocks.note: taken as written
CE is the Church of England
taken as written

explanation.surface: A skating show is a big hit with the churchgoers, and how!
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical performance on a rink with costumes and music is a spectacle staged by skaters.

clue.text: Name certain to describe one little pest

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw a line around it, so one word encircles the others

blocks.note: sure means certain
the Roman numeral for one
a gnat is a small biting fly

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to identify a small nuisance precisely.
explanation.walkthrough: Describe in its geometric sense, drawing round a figure, is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's handwritten autograph on a document is their written name, so a signature is a name.

clue.text: Run up from all directions

blocks.note: the four compass points south, east, west and north

explanation.surface: Someone sprints uphill from every side.
explanation.walkthrough: Run up is the dressmaking phrase for stitching something quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: To run up a garment is to make it quickly on a machine, so a run up dress has been stitched.

clue.text: Small egg on roll

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to egg someone on is to urge them

explanation.surface: A little egg sitting on a bread roll.
explanation.walkthrough: Egg on is a verb phrase, not a breakfast item placed on a roll.
explanation.definitionFit: Waves roll and surge alike, both describing a powerful forward heaving motion of water.

clue.text: Infinity of plane?

blocks.note: surface reading: a flat geometric plane stretching endlessly in every direction
setter's reading: the word planet with its last letter cut off, a globe deprived of its end

explanation.surface: A geometry question about whether a flat plane goes on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: Plane is planet lacking its final letter, so it is a world missing its end; the phrase also closes the Gloria Patri in Anglican prayer.
explanation.definitionFit: The liturgical phrase means for all eternity, everlasting, so it names endlessness or infinity.

clue.text: Sound of discharging weapon

indicators.note: sound of tells you to go by pronunciation rather than spelling

blocks.note: something oozy is seeping or discharging liquid

explanation.surface: The bang of a gun going off.
explanation.walkthrough: Discharging suggests firing a gun, but it means leaking fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israeli submachine gun named after its designer Uziel Gal is a well-known firearm.

clue.text: Fall carrying new ladder

indicators.note: something carrying a load holds it inside, so one word goes around the other

blocks.note: to sag is to droop or fall
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone tumbles while holding a brand-new ladder.
explanation.walkthrough: Ladder is the British word for a run in tights or stockings, not something to climb.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulled thread in hosiery that becomes a run, a ladder in British usage, is also called a snag.

clue.text: Odd wife that man rejected, of course

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the phrase's word is read backwards

blocks.note: W is the abbreviation for wife
the pronoun for that man as object
of course is an emphatic yes

explanation.surface: A strange wife turned that man down, naturally.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the less common spelling with an E; whimsy is fanciful, quaintly odd, and here the word is used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Whimsey or whimsy as an adjective describes something quaint, fanciful and peculiar, so it can mean strange.
